outcome: Still open on 11 October 2026: no proof or disproof has appeared since 26 January 2024, but the verified range was pushed from primes up to 10^13 (Odlyzko, 1993) to primes up to 10^14 (Plouffe, October 2025, independently matched by Colonna) and to a headline 1.5×10^15 (Colonna, March 2026); Chase, Hunter and Tao proved the leading-1 property for a Cramér random model and an inverse theorem for the deterministic sequence (arXiv 2607.08712, 9 July 2026), and state that the prime conjecture 'remains open'.
problem_asks: (1) The infinite sequence of primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... taken as the top row, not any single finite initial segment. (2) The unsigned forward difference operator applied repeatedly: each row is the list of absolute differences of consecutive entries of the row above, giving rows of decreasing length, one per depth k = 1, 2, 3, ... (3) The assertion that the first (leftmost) entry of every row after the first is 1 at every depth, equivalently that the left diagonal of the difference array is all ones after the first row. Parts that must each be addressed: (a) the leading-1 claim at every depth k, so unbounded depth is part of the claim; (b) the claim for the prime sequence itself, so it covers every initial length n of the primes, not only some; (c) it is stated for the primes specifically, so results on random or sieved analogues are about a different sequence. Wikipedia's January 2024 wording is 'the first term of every resulting row, after the start, is 1'.

events.what_happened: François Proth published the observations later called Gilbreath's conjecture in 1878 (cited by OEIS A393110 as F. Proth, Nouv. Corresp. Math. (1878); the journal itself was not opened). Wikipedia and several secondary sources say Proth also gave an attempted proof, later shown faulty. Chase (arXiv 2005.00530) argues that there is no evidence Proth published a proof, or even a false one, and calls the flawed-proof claim unfounded; Neil Sloane's 2023 notes are reported as agreeing (search snippet only; not opened).
events.delivers: At most an asserted pattern for all depths and all primes. Whether any argument was published is disputed; if one was, its content is not known from any source I opened.
events.doubts: The existence of a flawed published proof is contested: the Wikipedia article and several secondary sources say one was published and was faulty; Chase (2020) says there is no evidence of any published proof. The 1878 source was not opened, so neither side is verified here.
events.direction: Asserts the conjecture. Points the same way as the conjecture if an argument existed; no content verified.

events.what_happened: Andrew M. Odlyzko, 'Iterated absolute values of differences of consecutive primes', Math. Comp. 61(203) (1993), 373–380. Per the AMS abstract (seen in search results; the AMS page returned HTTP 403), the computation verifies the conjecture for all k up to π(10^13), which is 346,065,536,839 primes. The method uses a shortcut: if a row starts with 1 followed by n entries that are 0 or 2, the next n rows also start with 1. Odlyzko needed only the first 635 rows for the largest case (G(π(10^13)) = 635). The abstract also says the paper discusses heuristic evidence and that similar conjectures probably hold for many other sequences.
events.delivers: Verifies the leading-1 pattern for every initial segment of up to π(10^13) primes (the depth bound is G(π(10^13)) = 635). Restricted to that finite range; it says nothing about longer initial segments.
events.remains: The unbounded claim: every initial length beyond π(10^13), and every depth for those lengths.

events.what_happened: Leila Muney, 'Holes in Valid-Extension Sets of Finite Gilbreath Sequences', arXiv:2606.23721 (math.CO, cross-listed math.NT; v1 18 June 2026; v2 16 July 2026). Studies finite Gilbreath sequences (a sequence whose difference triangle has a leading 1 in every row below the top) and which integers can be appended to them. Shows that a previously proposed characterisation fails: valid-extension sets can have interior holes, the smallest at length 5 for (2,3,5,9,15). Gives an exact membership criterion and algorithm, a completeness criterion analogous to Brown's for subset sums, endpoint and reflection results, the minimum size of the set, a family with exponentially many components, and enumeration data to length 11. The introduction mentions the conjecture as open: 'The Gilbreath conjecture, which remains open, asserts that every initial segment of the primes is a Gilbreath sequence.'

events.remains: All of problem_asks for the prime sequence: the paper addresses the local extension problem for finite sequences, which the authors describe as a different question.
events.directly_checkable: The length-5 example (2,3,5,9,15) is a small finite case that can be checked by hand. The enumeration data through length 11 is machine-generated.
events.direction: Neither supports nor refutes the prime claim: it concerns finite Gilbreath sequences, and treats the prime conjecture as motivation.
events.object: A finite sequence (2,3,5,9,15) whose valid-extension set has an interior hole at length 5, which shows that a previously proposed characterisation fails for finite Gilbreath sequences. It is not a prime-sequence object.

events.what_happened: Zachary Chase, Zach Hunter and Terence Tao, 'Gilbreath's conjecture: a Cramér random model and a deterministic analysis', arXiv:2607.08712 (primary math.CO; v1 submitted 9 July 2026, 28 pages, 8 figures; single version). Tao announced it on his blog on 11 July 2026, with a heuristic discussion. Main results, per the HTML text: Theorem 1.2: with independent geometric inputs with parameter 2/(2+log n), almost surely the left diagonal takes values in {0,1} after finitely many rows (a Cramér random model of the prime gaps). Theorem 1.6: for non-negative integer initial data bounded by 2^M, if the array has no long block of zeros and no long shallow {0,d}-valued block (d ≥ 2), then the bottom entry lies in {0,1} (described as an inverse theorem, conditional on a Cramér-type bound on prime gaps). The continuous (exponential-input) model: partial sums of the constants c_i are at least log(n+e); c_0..c_3 computed exactly; boundedness of the c_i not shown. The paper states 'This conjecture remains open' and notes that the verification covers 3.34×10^11 rows (a figure that does not match π(10^13) = 346,065,536,839; see summary). Tao's blog states the heuristic (average row maximum about log n, Cramér bound O(log² n)) and says making it rigorous is well beyond current technology.
events.delivers: (i) The leading-1 property holds almost surely in the Cramér random model, a changed question (random geometric inputs, not the primes). (ii) A deterministic inverse theorem, conditional on a Cramér-type bound on prime gaps, which identifies the only obstructions (long zero blocks or long {0,d} blocks) for initial data bounded by 2^M. (iii) Partial information on the continuous model's constants (partial sums bounded below; c_0..c_3). It does not prove the leading-1 claim for the primes, and does not show the obstructions are absent.
events.remains: The prime case itself (all of problem_asks for primes); the absence of long zero blocks and long shallow blocks for the primes (unproved); the Cramér-type bound (unproved).

Proposes a sieving methodology and 'reverse sieving'. Claimed results (per the HTML text read in full): Theorem 2.3 (Δ-periodic sieved sequences S3 and S8 built by sieving with primes up to 19 are successful; κ ≤ 8); Theorem 2.4 (period ∏(p_i − 1)); Theorem 2.5 (random-order prime sieving with κ distinct primes yields successful sequences for κ ≤ κ0, κ0 'yet to be determined'; general κ conjectured); Theorem 3.1 (length bounds for admissible sequences); Theorem 3.2 (a corridor of parameters containing the primes; for n = 11 only one failing sequence); Theorem 5.1 (magic twin primes). events.what_happened: Michael Ross, 'Empirical Structure of the Gilbreath Decay Constants', Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21326026 (published 12 July 2026; last modified 4 September 2026; listed author affiliation 'Researcher'). A Monte Carlo study to depth 8192 for the stationary continuous Gilbreath model of Chase, Hunter and Tao (top row independent standard exponentials), with exact values of c_4, c_5 and c_6 added; proposes the empirical law c_i ≈ C·λ^{s_2(i)}/i with λ about 1.14–1.20, where s_2(i) is the binary digit sum. Code is linked at github.com/michaelmross/Gilbreath (not opened). Tao's blog comments of 13 July 2026 include Tao's remark 'A quick check against our Monte Carlo calculation reveals an excellent fit', and an anonymous comment, linked by handle to the same GitHub account, reports the extension of c_4–c_6. Two comments signed 'Michael M. Ross' announce OEIS submissions; a 29 July comment announces A397880 and A395556 (OEIS entries not opened).
events.revisions: v1 only per the record (last modified 4 Sep 2026)
events.delivers: Numerical evidence about the decay constants c_i of the continuous Gilbreath model, not the prime sequence. An empirical law, not a theorem.

disputes.summary: Whether François Proth published a proof in 1878. Wikipedia and several secondary sources say he published an attempted proof later shown to be false; Chase (arXiv 2005.00530) argues there is no evidence of any published proof, true or false, and Sloane's 2023 notes agree (search snippet). The 1878 source was not opened.

The name. Odlyzko's 1993 abstract (AMS, seen in search results) says the conjecture is usually credited to Gilbreath but was due to Proth in the 19th century. Gilbreath's own 1958 presentation is the conventional attribution.

Priority for the 10^14 check. Colonna's page dates his G(π(10^14)) = 693 to 10/05/2025 (opened). Plouffe's arXiv paper (8 Oct 2025 v1) says he completed his run on 7 October and that Colonna had reached the same value slightly earlier (from a search snippet; not verified in the body). Both are independent computations.
Early checks: MathWorld gives Kilgrove and Ralston (1959) for m < 63,419; T5K says two of Gilbreath's students verified the first 64,419 rows. Not resolved; neither original was opened.

summary: I found no proof or disproof of Gilbreath's conjecture in the sources, and the authors of the one substantive 2026 preprint state the prime case remains open, so the status is 'open' with no change since 26 January 2024. Events in the window: (1) the verified range moved from primes up to 10^13 (Odlyzko, 1993, G = 635, Math. Comp.) to primes up to 10^14 (Plouffe, arXiv 2510.06688, 8 October 2025; Colonna's page gives the same G = 693 dated 5 October 2025, an independent computation) and then to a headline 1.5×10^15 (Colonna, dated 18 March 2026, where his page describes the run as interrupted at that date, so the completed range is not settled by that page). (2) Chase, Hunter and Tao (arXiv 2607.08712, v1 9 July 2026; Tao blog 11 July) prove that the leading-1 property holds almost surely in a Cramér random model (Theorem 1.2), and give a deterministic inverse theorem (Theorem 1.6) that is conditional on a Cramér-type bound on prime gaps and reduces failure to long zero blocks or long {0,d} blocks; the prime case is not proved. Their predecessor is Chase's random analogue (arXiv 2005.00530, posted 1 May 2020, Math. Ann. 388(3) 2024 per Wikipedia). (3) Granville (arXiv 2607.04166, 5 July 2026) claims a sieving approach with partial results on sieved and random-order variants; the text reads its prime case as 'remains fully open'; I found no engagement. (4) Muney (arXiv 2606.23721, 18 June 2026) on finite Gilbreath sequences, which is a different question. (5) Ross (Zenodo 21326026, 12 July 2026) gives Monte Carlo numerics for the continuous model's constants, which Tao's blog comments say fit their Monte Carlo. (6) Shimizu (Zenodo 23160565, 5 October 2026) reproduces Odlyzko's 10^13 result and says it is not a new bound. Older items are recorded as events: Proth 1878 (disputed proof), Kilgrove and Ralston 1959, Eppstein 2011 (non-prime counterexamples), Gilbreath 2011 (not opened), Bhat, Cobeli and Zaharescu 2023 (quasi-periodicity; not on the conjecture), Agama 2021 (no result stated), and Salvia 2013 (withdrawn). AI involvement: four records name or describe AI use. (a) Chase, Hunter and Tao acknowledge 'Gemini was used to generate the code for Figure 1.' This is peripheral (figure code), so it is recorded here and not in ai.systems; the HTML was read in full and no other AI mention was found. The Pith AI referee review (model glm-5.2, T0) is an automated review, not a human reading, and says 'No human expert has reviewed this paper yet.' (b) Muney's acknowledgements state: 'This project made use of AI tools during the exploratory stage, including computational experimentation, conjecture generation, and preliminary drafting.' No system is named, so ai.systems is empty; 'conjecture generation' is the sentence a later pass would weigh, though the theorems concern finite sequences. (c) Shimizu's README and Zenodo record state 'AI-assisted (Claude, Anthropic; OpenAI Codex).' The record does not say what was assisted. I entered both names in ai.systems because the quote is generic and the computation is the artefact, but the reproduced result is Odlyzko's old one; this is a close call. (d) Granville, Plouffe, Colonna and Ross: no AI mention in the text read. For Plouffe only the abstract and metadata were readable (the HTML was 404 and the PDF binary), so that is weaker evidence. ProofAtlas, an 'AI-first' platform, hosts a Gilbreath 'collaboration' page with status 'Open conjecture', no proof claim, no named contributors and computations 'reported unreproduced'; it is not an event. The AI-focused searches found no AI-credited proof, counterexample or verification for this conjecture. Numerical discrepancies to note: Chase–Hunter–Tao and Wikipedia give 'first 3.34×10^11 rows', while π(10^13) = 346,065,536,839 ≈ 3.46×10^11; the sources do not reconcile these. Close calls: whether the Cramér random-model theorem counts as a changed question (by §2.1, yes, since it is a different sequence); whether finite verifications of a universal claim move anything the problem asks for (the judging pass decides); and whether the Shimizu AI disclosure is load-bearing.
competing_reading: The strongest case for counting 2026 as real progress: Chase, Hunter and Tao reduce the deterministic conjecture to two named obstructions (long zero runs and long shallow {0,d} blocks under a Cramér-type bound), a reframing that a referee could regard as a partial result on the deterministic analysis rather than a changed question; Tao is a co-author, the paper is a math.CO preprint and the blog gives a heuristic for plausibility. The opposing reading is that the random-model result is a different sequence, the inverse theorem is conditional on an unproved bound, and the authors say the prime case remains open. For the verifications: Plouffe and Colonna are independent computations and could be read as moving the verified range of a claim, but the statement is universal, so finitely many verified initial segments change nothing about the claim itself. For the AI record: Shimizu's 'AI-assisted (Claude, Anthropic; OpenAI Codex)' could be read as AI involvement in a computation, or as incidental code help for a reproduction of a 1993 result; Muney's 'conjecture generation' could be read as load-bearing for finite-sequence theorems, but those are not about primes.
what_would_settle_it: For the verification range: Colonna's statement of the completed range after 18 March 2026, and an independent reproduction of any value above 10^13 (the Shimizu package stops at 10^13). For the random-model and inverse results: a human referee or journal decision (only an AI T0 review exists), and whether the inverse theorem can be made unconditional. For the AI questions: the authors' account of what 'AI-assisted' covered in the Shimizu package, and whether any theorem in Muney's paper came from the 'conjecture generation' step. For Proth 1878: the 1878 Nouvelle Correspondance Mathématique text. For Granville: a referee or expert reading, or a journal decision. For the early checks: the original Kilgrove and Ralston (1959) paper and the T5K 'two students' source.

events.credibility_reason: Whether any proof was published is disputed (Wikipedia vs Chase 2020); the 1878 source was not opened.
Withdrawn by the author in v2 (19 July 2016) for flaws in the statistical method.
The page's 1.5x10^15 headline conflicts with its description of the run as interrupted, and it carries unreconciled captions (969 at 1.6931x10^15; G(Pi(6.150x10^15))=800).
The author labels central parts informal, conditional or partial ('None of this is proved yet'), and no engagement was found.

judgement.why: The statement is about the infinite prime sequence at every depth. Every computational check (Kilgrove–Ralston, Odlyzko, Plouffe, Colonna, Shimizu) only verifies finitely many initial segments, so I scored them instances (F5). Chase 2020, Chase–Hunter–Tao 2026 (Cramér random model), Granville (sieved sequences), Muney (finite Gilbreath sequences), Ross (continuous-model constants) and Eppstein (non-prime sequences) all settle changed questions, so I scored them variant. The Chase–Hunter–Tao inverse theorem is conditional on an unproved Cramér-type gap bound and leaves its obstructions open. That makes it a reduction, not a case, and its random-model theorem is the paper's main result. The authors themselves say the conjecture remains open. AI: Chase–Hunter–Tao used Gemini only for figure code, and Pith is an AI referee, so both count as none. Muney's disclosure names no system and the paper is a variant anyway. Shimizu's bare line 'AI-assisted (Claude, Anthropic; OpenAI Codex).' says nothing about any mathematics in a package that reproduces a 1993 computation, so it is none (F12); that event is discarded as instances in any case.
judgement.doubts: Shimizu's AI disclosure is generic. If Claude or Codex wrote the verification code, that is still not mathematics in the result. Muney's 'conjecture generation' disclosure may have contributed to theorems, but those theorems concern finite sequences, not the primes.
